summary: The Mixing ratio of air calculator turns the air temperature, the dew point and the station pressure into actual mixing ratio. It is built for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Mixing ratio of air calculator work?
sections.html:
The Mixing ratio of air calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports actual mixing ratio in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the temperature units for the chart); then you type in the air temperature, the dew point and the station pressure.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

sections.title: The formula behind the Mixing ratio of air calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Actual mixing ratio=(-38002367 × (10, 75 × dew point ÷ (10 × dew point + 2377) − 2) ÷ (61100 × (10, 75 × dew point ÷ (10 × dew point + 2377) − 2) − 100 × station pressure))
Saturation mixing ratio=(-38002367 × (10, 75 × air temperature ÷ (10 × air temperature + 2377) − 2) ÷ (61100 × (10, 75 × air temperature ÷ (10 × air temperature + 2377) − 2) − 100 × station pressure))
Relative humidity=((-38002367 × (10, 75 × dew point ÷ (10 × dew point + 2377) − 2) ÷ (61100 × (10, 75 × dew point ÷ (10 × dew point + 2377) − 2) − 100 × station pressure)) ÷ (-38002367 × (10, 75 × air temperature ÷ (10 × air temperature + 2377) − 2) ÷ (61100 × (10, 75 × air temperature ÷ (10 × air temperature + 2377) − 2) − 100 × station pressure)))
Actual vapor pressure=611 × (10, 75 × dew point ÷ (10 × dew point + 2377) − 2)
Saturated vapor pressure=611 × (10, 75 × air temperature ÷ (10 × air temperature + 2377) − 2)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • Pressure, opening in hectopascals
  • Pressure, opening in hectopascals
  • Pressure, opening in hectopascals
  • %, opening in percent

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Mixing ratio of air calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the air temperature, the dew point and the station pressure — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Mixing ratio of air calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns actual mixing ratio, derived from the air temperature, the dew point and the station pressure. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Mixing ratio of air calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the air temperature, the dew point and the station pressure, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter air temperature in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Air temperature opens in Celsius and the chip beside it offers 28 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Mixing ratio of air calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
